name: Waray (Waray-Waray)
variant: Waray of Leyte and Samar as spoken in Tacloban, the dialect called standard and used in broadcasting and education; h- forms of the markers and pronouns (hi, han, ha, hiya, hira, hin-o), with the s- forms (si, san, sa, siya, sira) heard elsewhere mentioned once; modern spelling without accent marks, hyphen for a glottal stop inside a word
script: Latin (Filipino alphabet; c, f, j, ñ, q, v, x, z only in loanwords; e and o mostly in loans and spelling); glottal stop inside a word written with a hyphen; left to right
basis: No Waray syllabus or textbook could be opened: lesson order follows Lang App's Cebuano plan (itself from Bunye and Yap, Cebuano for Beginners, UH Press 1971, whose contents I opened) and common course practice, with every Waray form taken from Tramp's 1991 Waray grammar and dictionary, English Wikipedia, Wikibooks and Romualdez's 1908 Samar-Leyte grammar; 27 A1 lessons
src: George Dewey Tramp Jr., Waray-Waray (Leyte-Samar) dictionary with grammar (preface dated 1991), PDF on zorc.net: read through a fetch tool's extracts of the first 100,000 of about 1.77 million characters only: contents, numbers, grammar paragraphs 1-33 (pronoun table ako, ikaw / ka, hiya / siya, kita, kami, kamo, hira / sira with genitive nakon / ko, nimo / mo, niya and preposed akon, imo, iya, aton, amon, ira; demonstratives adi, ini, iton, adto; markers hi / ni / kan, an / han / ha; verb affixes -um-, mag- / nag-, -in- / gin-, -an, i-; the palit conjugation table, partly garbled in the text (nagpalit, ginpalit, ginpalitan, papaliton, palita!, makakapalit); maka- / naka- for 'can'; diri for present and future, waray for past and 'there isn't'; gusto / karuyag, kinahanglan; mas and labi; ada / aada 'there is'; ala / alas with Spanish numbers (alas dosi); aga; actor-focus future ma- for -um- verbs and mag- with a doubled syllable, present na- and nag- with a doubled syllable (paragraphs 5, 9, 27, 31, read from garbled tables)), and the Samar (Catbalogan) dialect section heading. The dictionary entries were not read

English Wikipedia, Waray language (current page and a 2021 archived copy whose grammar section is empty): names (Waray, Waray-Waray, Winaray, Binisaya), about 3.6 million native speakers (2015 census), Tacloban as the standard dialect, other dialects (Northern Samar, Calbayog, Catbalogan, Abuyog, Culaba-Biliran), ISO war, KWF orthography, case-marker table (an, an mga, han / san, ha / sa, hi / si, ni, kan; hira / sira, nira, kira), demonstrative and question-word lists (ano, hin-o, diin, san-o, kay ano), numbers usa ... napulo and Spanish numbers from 11 up
Wikibooks, Wikijunior: Languages/Waray: greetings (Kumusta?, Maupay man, salamat; Maupay nga aga, Maupay udto, Maupay nga kulop, Maupay nga gabii), Damo nga salamat, Waray sapayan, oo / diri, numbers

Norberto Romualdez, Bisayan Grammar and Notes on Bisayan Rhetoric and Poetics and Filipino Dialectology (1908; Project Gutenberg ebook 69603): read through a fetch-tool extract of the first 100,000 of about 189,000 characters: it describes the Samar and part-Leyte ('Samareño') dialect; active voice future ma- (másurat), present na- (násurat), past -inm- (inmurát); direct passive sinúsurat, sinurát, susuratón; pronouns acó, icáo / ca, hiyá / siyá, quitá, camí, camó, hirá / sirá; articles an, in, hi / si, ni, han / san, mg̃a. 1908 spelling, respelled in the titles

Swarthmore College LING073 student wiki, Waray and English / Contrastive Grammar: a student project, but the only source I read for the question particle ba (Maampo ba hi Bong?) and for nag- with a doubled first syllable in modern spelling (nag-aaram); also nga, mga, hiya, hira, ini, iton
Wilmo Orejola, Learning Waray vol. 1, sample on academia.edu: iton and amo standing for 'is' (Wilmo iton akon ngaran), kita / kami, verb affixes listed without paradigms
Omniglot, Waray-Waray page: where spoken, dialect list, Tacloban dialect as the standard used in media and education
Wiktionary, Appendix: Cebuano-Waray-Waray relations: pronouns ako, kami, kita, ikaw, kamo, imo, inyo; waray 'none'

Not opened or not usable: Ethnologue / SIL entry for war, Wikivoyage Waray phrasebook (fetch failed), ABVD Waray word list (blocked), the Peace Corps Waray tapes and Madeja's reference grammar (seen only as search-result titles), a Cornell eCommons PDF from the search results (not opened), Ehnis 2025 on the g- prefix (opened; no paradigm)
note: No beginner course or syllabus for Waray was opened, so the order is my own, modelled on the Cebuano plan (a close relative) and on common course practice; only the forms come from the sources. From the sources: markers, pronouns, demonstratives, question words, numbers, greetings, actor-focus ma- / na- (Romualdez, Tramp, Swarthmore's maampo) and nag- / mag- with the doubled syllable (Tramp, Swarthmore), gin- / -on / gin-...-an with palit and surat, palita!, maka- / naka-, diri / waray, ada / aada, gusto / karuyag, kinahanglan, mas / labi, alas dosi, aga / udto / kulop / gabii, iton / amo as 'is'. The modern spellings masurat, nasurat, susuraton are my respelling of Romualdez's 1908 forms, and the exact use of ma- against mag- verbs in today's Tacloban speech must be checked with a speaker. Tramp marks mas as Spanish and dialectal and gives the native comparative infix -ru- (maupay > mauruupay); the course teaches mas as the easier form and writers may add -ru-. Own knowledge, not in what I read: the family words (nanay, tatay, bugto, anak), the drinking-water word tubig, didi (here; Wikipedia lists didi among 'here' forms but I took the pairing with didto from my own knowledge), pesos, and using 'pira' for prices (Tramp glosses pira only as 'how many'). Deliberately left out because no source I read confirmed them: may-ada / mayda, Tagpira?, Taga-diin ka?, the words for left and right, a word for 'please', and ayaw for negative commands (Tramp lists ayaw only as an interjection). The Wikibooks phrase 'Asa ka gikan?' was not used (it looks Cebuano). The pronoun ak: Tramp's table lists it as a short possessive but his own example (kun pumalit ak) uses it as 'I', as Tacloban speech does in my knowledge; writers must confirm. The Tramp conjugation extract is garbled in places, so only clearly labelled forms were used. Variant: h- forms throughout, following Tramp's main column and Wikipedia's first-listed forms; whether Tacloban itself prefers h- or s- forms in every case must be checked with a speaker. Voice: war-PH is the BCP-47 shape; no device voice was checked and probably none exists. Writers must check every Waray word with a first-language speaker from Leyte.
hardest: Verb focus and aspect: actor-focus ma- / na- and mag- / nag- against goal-focus -on / gin- (masurat, nagpalit; papaliton, ginpalit), with a doubled first syllable for 'is doing' and 'will' (nag-aaram, papaliton)
Three pronoun sets (ako, nakon / ko, akon) and the markers an / hi, han / ni, ha / kan
Two words for 'not': diri for now and later, waray for the past and for 'there isn't' (Waray, the language's name, means 'none')
Spanish numbers from 11 up and for the clock (alas dosi) next to native usa, duha, tulo

items: Sounds and spelling: three vowel sounds (a, i, u; e and o in loans), ng, the glottal stop
Greetings: Maupay nga aga, Maupay udto, Maupay nga kulop, Maupay nga gabii, Kumusta?, Maupay man
Thanks, yes and no: Damo nga salamat, Waray sapayan, oo, diri
adi, ini, iton, adto: this and that; Ano ini?
Pronouns ako / ak, ikaw / ka, hiya and the markers an and hi
Introducing yourself: akon ngaran, iton and amo for 'is' (… iton akon ngaran)
Question words: ano, hin-o, diin, san-o, pira, kay ano; yes-no questions with ba
We, you all, they: kita and kami, kamo, hira; mga for more than one
Possession: akon, imo, iya before the noun, nakon / ko, nimo / mo, niya after it; han and ni
Describing words and the linker nga: maupay nga aga, damo nga salamat
There is and there isn't: ada / aada and waray
Numbers: usa, duha, tulo … napulo, and the Spanish numbers used from 11 up
Prices and buying: pira, pesos, and the verb palit (buy)
Actor-focus verbs 1: ma- (will) and na- (does, is doing): masurat, nasurat; Maampo ba hi Bong?
Actor-focus verbs 2: nag- (did), and nag- / mag- with the first syllable doubled (is doing, will do): nagpalit, nag-aaram
diri and waray: not (now, later) and did not
Times of day and the clock: aga, udto, kulop, gabii; alas dosi
gusto / karuyag and kinahanglan: want and need
Eating and drinking: kaon, inom, tubig
Where things are: ha (at, in), diin; didi, didto
Going places: ngain? (where to?), ha, adto
Goal-focus verbs: gin- (did) and a doubled syllable + -on (will): ginpalit, papaliton, susuraton
-an verbs: ginpalitan (bought from or for someone)
Comparing: mas maupay, and labi ka- for 'most' (labi kahalaba)
Can: maka- / naka-; diri maka- (cannot), waray maka- (could not)
